d62c4bdbdaf416b79e6d1ee1.title_original: Sample-Preserving Search-to-Decision Reduction for Noisy Linear Equations over Large Moduli
d62c4bdbdaf416b79e6d1ee1.excerpt: arXiv:2610.12913v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Noisy Linear Equations problem involves finding the solution to a random linear system over a finite field given noisy evaluations. This is a generalisation of various learning problems widely used in cryptography, including Learning with Errors (LWE), Learning with Rounding (LWR), and Learning Parity with Noise (LPN). We present a new sample-preserving search-to-decision reduction for Noisy Linear Equations that has complexity $\mathrm{poly}(n,m,\log q, q/\sigma)$, where $n$ is the dimension of the secret, $m$ is the number of samples, $q$ is the modulus, and $\sigma$ is the magnitude of the noise (defined suitably for the kind of noise involved). In particular, this implies search-to-decision reductions for LWE and LWR that run in time $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ even if the modulus $q$ is exponentially large, as long as the noise-to-modulus ratio $\sigma/q$ is non-negligible. Our reduction works for prime moduli $q$. If $q$ is composite, it instead produces a list that contains a small multiple of the solution. Prior to this work, known search-to-decision reductions for LWE and LWR either did not preserve the parameters of the problem (i.e., $m$, $n$, $\sigma$, and $q$), or had complexity that scaled polynomially with either $\sigma$ or the largest prime factor of $q$.

423e809efc118265092ae53b.title_original: AgentValve: Sybil-Resilient Payment Authorization for Permissionless AI Markets
423e809efc118265092ae53b.excerpt: arXiv:2610.12948v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents increasingly select and pay service providers without human review. In emerging permissionless markets, however, adversaries can create inexpensive identities and fabricate feedback to inflate provider reputation, making reputation-based payment authorization vulnerable to Sybil attacks and exposing clients to unbounded financial loss. This paper presents AgentValve, a protocol for Sybil-resilient payment authorization in permissionless AI markets. AgentValve builds on a trust network that represents reputation as finite capacity in a directed graph and authorizes payments through trust paths with sufficient available capacity. A smart contract atomically reserves the capacity supporting each admitted payment, bounding honest agents' payment exposure by the capacity they extend into the adversarial region, and thus creating identities or interactions entirely within that region cannot increase this bound. To limit capacity depletion by malicious senders, AgentValve combines payment-backed capacity creation with bounded route length, preventing attackers from depleting honest capacity without incurring corresponding payment costs. AgentValve further decouples off-chain route discovery from on-chain verification and introduces a witness-commit mechanism that reduces route verification to linear work while requiring only constant persistent state per admitted payment. We implement a AgentValve prototype and evaluate it us

2ab0c4eac5cb8ae20a86b508.title_original: WaveMark: Robust Wavelet-Domain Image Watermarking for Diffusion Models
2ab0c4eac5cb8ae20a86b508.excerpt: arXiv:2610.12952v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Image watermarking enables provenance tracing for photorealistic images generated by diffusion models. However, state-of-the-art (SOTA) removal attacks can suppress embedded signals with little perceptual degradation. This vulnerability limits the effectiveness of watermarks for intellectual property protection and misuse attribution. We propose WaveMark, a novel wavelet-domain watermarking method that embeds messages in a diffusion model's initial noise. To support robust recovery from perturbed carriers, WaveMark distributes keyed replicas of message bits across spatial positions, wavelet orientations, and scales. Each carrier groups coefficients from four latent channels and encodes a randomized bit through magnitude projection, providing an explicit decoding margin. We evaluate WaveMark with SD2.1 on SDP and MS-COCO Captions under 14 attacks. WaveMark achieves 100.0% bit accuracy (BA) without attacks, while maintaining image quality comparable to the evaluated baselines. Under SOTA MarkNull and MarkNull-A, it retains over 88% BA, outperforming all baselines.

9cf022621fc2592d8ab34a5b.title_original: Post-Quantum Session Establishment for Matter over Thread: Message Size, Transport, and Protocol Options
9cf022621fc2592d8ab34a5b.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Matter's first post-quantum change protects device attestation with ML-DSA, but its operational handshake, CASE, still derives session keys from P-256 ECDH, so recorded traffic can be decrypted once a quantum computer exists. We quantify the cost of moving CASE to ML-KEM and post-quantum signatures over Thread, where frames carry at most 127 bytes and a Matter message at most 1178 bytes. A byte-exact model of the CASE messages shows that a drop-in ML-KEM-768/ML-DSA-44 handshake grows from 1.6 kB to 22.8 kB and that no fully post-quantum configuration built from FIPS 203/204/205 algorithms fits the message limit. A Monte Carlo model of multi-hop Thread, calibrated to OpenThread and Matter source constants, shows that sending these messages as fragmented IPv6 datagrams causes spurious retransmissions whenever a message and its reply outlast Matter's retransmission timer. At three to four hops the drop-in handshake then takes 1.8 to 2.6 times longer than with a selective-repeat block transfer, with or without interference, and up to 33% of handshakes with sleepy devices fail; raising the timers does not remove the effect. Caching certificate chains and authenticating the device with a pre-distributed ML-KEM key reduce the handshake to 6.1 kB and 44 ms of device computation. 1c43a333ac61d2e3090c4330.title_original: Provably Subexponential Algorithms for Bounded-Error LWE with Few Samples
1c43a333ac61d2e3090c4330.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13043v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that a variant of the Wagner/BKW-style algorithm for LWE of Kirchner and Fouque [KF15] solves decision and search LWE with secrets of size $n$ over prime moduli $q=n^{\kappa+o(1)}$, for any fixed $\kappa>0$, with errors bounded by $\exp((\ln n)^{o(1)})$, in time $2^{O(n/\ln\ln n)}$ given $n+O(n/\ln\ln n)$ original samples. Further, if each coordinate of the secret is also bounded by $\exp((\ln n)^{o(1)})$, the same time bound holds with errors bounded by $n^{o(1)}$ and only $O(n/\ln\ln q)$ samples. Earlier, it was known that Kirchner and Fouque's algorithm could solve LWE with these parameters in subexponential time with a much larger number of samples $m = \Omega(n\log{n})$ [HKM18]. Ducas et al. [DEL25] showed that an adaptation of this algorithm could solve the corresponding dual, the $\mathrm{SIS}^{\infty}$ problem, with a suitable norm bound $q/\operatorname{polylog}(n)$ and $m=n+\omega(n/\ln\ln n)$ variables in subexponential time. Whereas their analysis involves interpreting the algorithm in terms of chains of lattices, our approach is quite elementary and is based on bounding the lower moments of a Fourier statistic.

a4c6055fd6645bd3aa6707ec.title_original: Space Over Statistic, Retraining Over Ranking: Auditing Training Labels Under Label-Only Backdoors
a4c6055fd6645bd3aa6707ec.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13051v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Some backdoor attacks never touch an image. FLIP only changes labels: on CIFAR-10, flipping 3% of them makes a ResNet-32 send 99.7% of triggered source-class images to the attacker's class. The usual defenses look for the poison inside a model trained on those same labels. So when they struggle, is the problem the test they run, or the space they run it in? We answer with a controlled swap: we keep the test, the labels and the metric fixed, change only the feature space, and judge each defense by retraining the victim on what it keeps. The space decides. On dog$\to$cat the same nearest-neighbor check scores AUROC 0.546 on the poisoned model's features, 0.967 on frozen DINOv2 features that never saw a label, and 0.995 on the same network trained on clean labels, an oracle control rather than a defense. We reproduce SPECTRE, the defense FLIP's authors recommend, to 90.94 / 0.97 against its published 91.47 / 1.7, then price it: on truck$\to$deer it deletes 20% of every class, while a prototype audit on the frozen features deletes 6% for higher clean accuracy and lower attack success. On three harder pairs that audit leaves about a quarter of the attack standing. A count read off encoder geometry and clean labels, before any attack is run, separates the pair where the audit removes the attack from those where it only partly does, though on a single zero-count pair. Three results warn against the easy story. A better detection score

9ca6406df6c9ec22d1abaa95.title_original: CAPE - Context-Aware Prioritization Engine for Vulnerability Scoring and Management
9ca6406df6c9ec22d1abaa95.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vulnerability patching is critical for safeguarding an enterprise's software ecosystem from cyber attacks. However, patching requires adequate preparation for potential system downtime and for unforeseen effects of the patched software on a live system. Thus, effective risk mitigation requires prioritization strategies that explicitly account for the operational context of the affected software. While vulnerability prioritization based on Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS), Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) and CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, can help, their differing goals and methodologies often lead to inconsistent, context-unaware decisions resulting in mis-allocated remediation efforts. In this work, we present the Context-Aware Prioritization Engine (CAPE), a vulnerability analysis framework that enriches each vulnerability scanner report of vulnerabilities (CVEs) with deployment-specific evidence. This evidence is used to perform vulnerability reachability, centrality, and exploitability analysis, producing a ranked priority score for the effective distribution of remediation effort. We evaluate CAPE on 30 open-source agentic applications comprising 6,138 scanner-reported CVEs. Our evaluation shows that a significant majority of CVEs are not reachable and exploitable which results in significant disparities between CAPE and context-free baselines - the CVSS, EPSS, and KEV. It also shows

954d078746726fcfc765bc2b.title_original: The Limits of Query Monitoring against Distributed Model Extraction
954d078746726fcfc765bc2b.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13083v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model providers now face distillation campaigns run through thousands of accounts, each of which looks like an ordinary user. When network and payment metadata cannot link those accounts, the only evidence left is what they ask. We study what a provider can and cannot learn from those queries alone, using one million real chat turns for development and 17 later weeks that no design choice touched for a single frozen evaluation. The answer is set less by anything specific to extraction than by benign coordination: a campaign is visible only if it is more distinctive than the most distinctive group of ordinary users in the same week. We make this precise, show that a small but positive difference between campaign and users buys a detection time rather than detectability, and identify the campaign that is hardest to detect. Empirically, a calibrated monitor catches naive distributed extraction that per-account monitors miss (0.86-1.00 of weeks), and one variant - selecting accounts that move together after discounting how topical each one is - still catches campaigns padded with natural text (0.50-0.96 of weeks) where the other two spectral detectors catch none. Distilling each campaign into a small student shows that, in our testbed, campaigns that evaded every detector kept at most 42% of the capability of a detectable one. The limits are equally concrete: a campaign that ramps up slowly poisons every detector's calibration, beni

e10437f835bfb0f483301cc8.title_original: Safety Graph: When Safety Responses Become Attack Surfaces in Cyber-Physical Systems
e10437f835bfb0f483301cc8.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13086v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern industrial control systems (ICS) are susceptible to cyber attacks triggering safety failures in the operational technology (OT) layer. The traditional way to mitigate any failure in OT is to implement safety responses. However, we show in this work that these responses can open up new attack surfaces, thereby vastly expanding the scope of lateral movement. Existing frameworks model cyber-to-physical escalation but provide no mechanism to reason about how these safety responses to OT-failures can trigger new cascading cyber attacks in the Information Technology (IT) layer. A complexity and scalability analy

d3620fa3282ee60cc1bf7fa7.title_original: Understanding Verification Vulnerabilities in Cross-chain Bridges: An Empirical Study
d3620fa3282ee60cc1bf7fa7.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13170v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the rapid development of blockchain technology, numerous heterogeneous blockchains have emerged, each featuring distinct architectures, consensus mechanisms, and application ecosystems. Cross-chain bridges have consequently become a critical infrastructure component, typically relying on smart contracts to facilitate message passing and asset transfers across heterogeneous blockchains. Unlike single-chain contracts, bridge contracts introduce additional verification logic to validate external-chain data, such as state proofs, message sender identities, and signatures. However, correctly implementing such logic is challenging. We refer to vulnerabilities that violate the security guarantees of cross-chain verification as Cross-chain Verification Vulnerabilities (CVVs). To characterize CVVs, we conduct the first systematic empirical study of this vulnerability class. By analyzing 588 security audit reports from 36 real-world cross-chain bridge projects, we derive 11 CVV patterns and organize them into 5 high-level categories according to the affected verification properties. Following this taxonomy, we construct a CVV dataset containing 830 vulnerability instances across 786 contract files. The dataset establishes mappings among audit reports, audited source-code versions, affected source files, and CVV-pattern labels. We then assess existing detection approaches. Current tools provide limited documented coverage of CVV patte

3a91b9805f8686543af7d35c.title_original: Understanding and Mitigating Cross-Session Attacks via Persistent Artifacts in Agent Skill Composition
3a91b9805f8686543af7d35c.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13227v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent skills extend the capabilities of AI agents by bundling instructions, code, and resources into reusable packages. During skill execution, agents may produce or modify artifacts, such as files, configurations, and cached data, that are reused by other skills in later sessions. Since these artifacts can persist across sessions and later be accessed by other skills, they introduce a new attack surface that can be exploited to influence subsequent executions. However, the security risks arising from such cross-session skill interactions remain largely unexplored. In this work, we investigate cross-session composition attacks in skill-based AI agents and develop a runtime defense against them. Specifically, we characterize three attack mechanisms, namely Instruction Propagation (IP), Data Boundary Violation (DBV), and Evidence Poisoning (EP), through which malicious effects propagate across skill executions via persistent artifacts. To evaluate whether existing agents can resist these attacks while completing legitimate tasks, we construct SkillRelayBench, a benchmark of 270 adversarial cases drawn from 30 cross-session skill-composition scenarios across ten domains. Our evaluation of seven models across Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, and Claude Code reveals attack success rates (ASR) ranging from 46.7% to 77.4% and attack chain success rates (ACSR) ranging from 35.6% to 61.1%. 3a91b9805f8686543af7d35c.title_ko: 에이전트 스킬 구성에서 영구 아티팩트를 통한 교차 세션 공격 이해 및 완화
3a91b9805f8686543af7d35c.summary_ko: 연구진은 AI 에이전트가 세션 간에 재사용하는 영구 아티팩트를 악용해 발생하는 교차 세션 구성 공격의 위험성을 조사하고 새로운 런타임 방어 기법을 제안했다. 새로운 벤치마크 평가 결과 기존 모델들은 높은 공격 성공률을 보였으나, 제안된 'SkillRelayGuard' 방어벽을 통해 공격 성공률을 크게 낮추고 정상적인 작업 완료율을 높일 수 있었다.

ae589bf80ccda56cc3d4eb73.title_original: Quantization-Tolerant Gradient Auditing for Active Inference-Attack Detection in Federated Learning
ae589bf80ccda56cc3d4eb73.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inside a federated learning system a participant can quietly study the shared model and learn about others' private data. The usual defense, differential privacy, often adds so much noise that the model is no longer worth training. In cross-silo FL, where participants are a few accountable organizations and the server is trusted, we ask whether the server can instead interrogate clients. Each round it sends a secret challenge batch and asks every client to return a checksum of the gradient that batch induces, together with a timing. A client that mutated the model state, as an active generative-adversarial-network discriminator attacker does, returns a wrong checksum. We make this checksum robust to benign cross-platform floating-point non-determinism with a quantized fingerprint compared under a small tolerance. It flags two distinct active attacks at a true-positive rate of $1.0$ with no false positives on the checksum axis, stable across the fingerprint's parameters and up to $50$ clients at malicious ratios to $40\%$, for $32\,\mathrm{ms}$ of server work and $4.35\,\mathrm{kB}$ per response. Against a purely passive attacker the only signal is timing, and it is not robust: a cohort-relative test detects only in low-jitter conditions while a false-positive-free per-client baseline is blind, so no configuration delivers both. An attacker that answers the challenge on an untouched copy of the model while tampering with a replic

85b4f077bde14e7ee301a42a.title_original: Secrets in Preamble: Practical and Robust PHY Information Hiding for Wi-Fi
85b4f077bde14e7ee301a42a.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13367v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physical layer (PHY) information hiding refers to the concealment of secrets within PHY waveforms without compromising the integrity of the primary communication link, thereby enabling critical applications such as covert communication, PHY steganography, and watermarking. The widespread deployment of Wi-Fi has motivated substantial research interest in hiding secrets within Wi-Fi waveforms. However, existing Wi-Fi information hiding approaches suffer from two limitations: restricted steganographic capacity and insufficient robustness against environmental variations, both of which severely constrain practical deployment. This work proposes to embed secrets within the Wi-Fi legacy short training field (L-STF). The designed method preserves the autocorrelation properties of Wi-Fi L-STF, ensuring that packet detection and coarse frequency offset compensation functionalities remain uncompromised. The secret embedding and extraction processes employ a pair of neural networks designed to learn optimal embedding rules and maximize steganographic capacity. We developed a prototype system and conducted comprehensive experiments across both indoor and outdoor environments. Experimental results show that our method can reliably embed 46 secret bits within Wi-Fi packets across diverse channel conditions, achieving significantly enhanced steganographic capacity and environmental robustness. The hardware prototype study validates the feasibi

f61b4a46d7bb5fdf1f686171.title_original: Towards Safe World Models: Risks, Defenses, and Evaluation
f61b4a46d7bb5fdf1f686171.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13372v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: World models support planning, control, learning from imagined experience, and model-mediated evaluation by predicting action-conditioned consequences. Their safety cannot be inferred from predictive accuracy alone: errors in observations, state and memory, dynamics, evaluation, execution, or feedback can propagate into unsafe decisions and persist through updates. This work organizes the literature on world-model safety around a six-stage lifecycle covering data and observations, state and memory, dynamics and imagination, evaluation and planning, action and control, and feedback and update. We synthesize non-adversarial failures, attacks, defenses, evaluation protocols, benchmarks, and deployment conditions, and distinguish evidence directness from outcome level. The current evidence corpus contains 163 cited works. We use the framework to identify where claims are supported, where attribution remains unresolved, and which measurements are needed to connect model-level behavior to closed-loop and operational safety.

4a0116980aaf91869af577e1.title_original: EviRepair: Evidence-Driven Agents for Reliable Vulnerability Repair
4a0116980aaf91869af577e1.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13491v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled agent-based approaches for repository-level automated vulnerability repair (AVR), showing promising repair capabilities. However, an important issue has received limited attention: how can we ensure that the evidence generated during the repair process is reliable enough to support accurate vulnerability understanding and patch generation? In this paper, we propose EviRepair, an evidence-driven multi-agent framework for repository-level AVR. EviRepair introduces evidence review into the repair process by enabling agents to collaboratively collect vulnerability evidence, verify evidence consistency, and construct a reviewed vulnerability model for patch synthesis and validation. Extensive experiments on PatchEval and SecBench benchmarks with multiple agent frameworks and LLMs demonstrate that EviRepair consistently outperforms existing agent-based baselines, achieving average improvements of 16.37% and 40.33% in resolved rates on PatchEval and SecBench, respectively. Codes are available at https://github.com/lly-s/EviRepair

3c47b939bbd894fc0b84501d.title_original: A Systematic Study of Security Enforcement at Android Inter-Component Boundaries
3c47b939bbd894fc0b84501d.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13597v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Android's inter-process communication (IPC) mechanisms (Activities, Services, BroadcastReceivers, ContentProviders, and URI scheme handlers) form the primary interface between applications and between applications and the system. We present a systematic study of security enforcement comprising 120 evaluations (99 inter-component interface evaluations across five interface categories, 10 platform security-control evaluations, and 11 dedicated positive controls) in over 30 Google and AOSP packages on Android 17 (API 37). Using an expected-versus-observed framework under a zero-permission attacker model, we evaluate whether each boundary's enforcement mechanism functions as designed. We find 97 enforcement gaps (80.8%) and 23 enforcement holds (19.2%). From these observations, we derive a 14-category enforcement gap taxonomy organized across manifest, code, platform, and architectural layers. Within our purposively selected corpus, observed enforcement outcomes differ substantially across interface categories: evaluated Activities and BroadcastReceivers exhibit a 100% gap rate, while ContentProviders, which benefit from framework-provided defenses such as setStrict(), achieve a 27.6% holds rate. We find that all seven evaluated platform compatibility changes with security intent are either disabled or gated at a targetSdkVersion that none of the applications in our evaluated corpus targets. We document 18 custom URI scheme registra

7f638743275234bec4d44f66.title_original: APEX-Harm: Evaluating Agent Safety in Shared Professional Workspaces
7f638743275234bec4d44f66.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Professional agents increasingly work through command-line interfaces and multiple tools over shared workspaces containing files, messages, and business applications. These environments create safety risks that are difficult to capture with attacks placed at a single, known read location. We introduce APEX-Harm, a benchmark for evaluating prompt and script injection against long-horizon agents performing finance, consulting, and legal tasks in large workspaces. Each task contains 115 to 328 files, together with email, calendar, chat, document, spreadsheet, PDF, and code-execution tools exposed through MCP servers. The benchmark includes six attack categories covering static and dynamic injections, task-specific script replacement, and attacker-provided generic scripts, and evaluates attack success, exposure, and task performance. We evaluate 12 frontier models on 180 task instances per model. Opus 5 and Sonnet 5 have the lowest overall attack success rates (8% and 20%), while task-specific script replacement and attacker-provided generic script attacks remain substantially more effective, averaging 81-84% and 73% attack success, respectively. Gemini 3.8 Flash achieves the highest mean task score (0.877) while still exhibiting a 33% attack success rate. These results show that completing the requested task is not sufficient evidence of safe behavior: an agent can produce a correct deliverable while also performing an unauthorized

a00b95c292007e48f2e69417.title_original: ToFu: Exploiting and Fuzzing the LLM-Orchestrator-Tool Trust Boundary
a00b95c292007e48f2e69417.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13651v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that interact with external software through tools, with an orchestration layer translating model outputs into structured tool invocations. This architecture creates an LLM-orchestrator-tool trust boundary where tool semantics may go unenforced and LLM-generated arguments may be incorrectly treated as trusted. We present ToFu, a tool-aware framework that automatically derives semantic security checks for LLM tools from their existing metadata and a CWE-guided sanitizer corpus. ToFu specializes these checks to individual tools and automatically generates fuzzing harnesses and semantic oracles using runtime introspection and outcome sanitization. We evaluated ToFu across 273 MCP servers containing 3405 tools and identified verified bugs corresponding to CWE weakness classes in 343 tools across 118 of the servers. Our findings show that real-world tools frequently fail to enforce their documented input semantics, making it unsafe to treat LLM-generated arguments as trusted.

49940e79df5a27b7feb42320.title_original: Decision-Focused Learning for Cyber-Physical Risk-Aware Power Grid Operations
49940e79df5a27b7feb42320.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13853v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Power grid cyber-physical security requires intrusion detection methods that account for the operational consequences of detection errors. However, the existing intrusion detection approaches primarily focus on the predictive performance of learning algorithms, while downstream operational costs are often optimized independently, which can lead to inferior operational performance. To help alleviate this problem, we propose a novel optimization-learning cyber-physical-risk-informed framework that communicates iteratively to minimize power grid operational costs. This framework translates machine learning prediction errors into power grid operational cyber-physical-risk costs. Experimental results on two power grid operation datasets, Industrial Control System (ICS) Cyber Attack and Sherlock, show that the proposed approach improves power grid operation costs compared with the traditional approach.

dfa50ff487fb8629400d469b.title_original: Byzantine-Resilient Federated Large Language Model via Hypergraph Message Passing
dfa50ff487fb8629400d469b.excerpt: arXiv:2610.12711v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Federated Large Language Models (FedLLMs) are promising to deliver privacy-preserving, collaborative intelligence. The decentralized training process is vulnerable to Byzantine attacks that corrupt semantic consistency and factual resilience through malicious model updates. This paper presents a new resilience strategy that prevents semantically corrupted knowledge from propagating during federated aggregation. A defense problem is formulated to jointly maximize global accuracy and suppress manipulated model updates, enabling trustworthy knowledge aggregation without accessing private local data. To strengthen the resilience of FedLLMs, we develop a novel Hypergraph Message Passing Graph Autoencoder (HMP-GAE) framework, where low-rank model updates are represented as nodes in a hypergraph and high-order semantic relationships among multiple agents are exploited through iterative message passing. By leveraging historical checkpoints and cross-agent relational reasoning, HMP-GAE identifies and suppresses semantically inconsistent updates while preserving knowledge alignment among agents throughout federated training. HMP-GAE is implemented using Qwen-2.5 and Llama-3.2 as pretrained FedLLM backbones and evaluated on AG News and Yahoo! Answers datasets. Compared to existing defenses, HMP-GAE improves global accuracy by $1.21$\%, reduces final-model classification semantic entropy by $44.08$\%, and lowers perplexity by $13.34$\%. H

0e848ff23621f77e447eeefd.title_original: The False Allure of "Security by Obscurity": A Game-Theoretic Approach
0e848ff23621f77e447eeefd.excerpt: arXiv:2610.12858v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: "Security by obscurity," or the idea that hiding how a system works helps protect it from adversaries, has long been poorly regarded in the security community. Yet its intuitive appeal persists, and it has resurfaced repeatedly in industry practices and public debates over the years. The logic, on the one hand, is that open scrutiny of systems is the best way to find and respond to problems; and on the other hand, that too much openness can increase risk by giving adversaries a roadmap for attack. This isn't purely a technical question, but a human one: it's about how attackers and good-faith security researchers respond to openness in the real world. As such, security experts base their stance on decades of community experience; however, the field lacks empirical or theoretical foundations to back up these long-standing beliefs. We provide the first rigorous modeling of "security by obscurity," aiming to capture how rational actors will respond to openness or obscurity in fallible systems. We prove that in equilibrium under realistic model conditions, "obscured" systems are more likely to suffer successful attacks than "open" systems --- establishing theoretical support for the longstanding received wisdom.

60b448affd339411945dd574.title_original: LETHE: Defending against Unauthorized Image-to-Video Generation via Value Diversity Collapse
60b448affd339411945dd574.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13333v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Image-to-video (I2V) diffusion models can animate a single reference image into high-quality, subject-consistent videos, posing threats of misuse as anyone can turn personal photos into fabricated videos without consent. A promising solution is to proactively add an adversarial perturbation to the image before release, such that videos generated from it would be unfaithful or visually corrupted. However, due to an insufficient understanding of what governs how subsequent frames read the reference image in modern I2V models, existing protections struggle to offer strong protection under common perturbation budgets. In this paper, we approach the problem by exploring this underlying reading mechanism. Through a convex geometric analysis, we theoretically identify the spread of the reference value vectors as a key factor governing this reading process, and empirically find that even a mild contraction of this spread can severely degrade the generated video, making it an efficient lever for protection. Guided by this insight, we propose LETHE, a novel protection method that directly disrupts this reading process. LETHE pairs two complementary objectives, where a value collapse objective drives the reference value vectors toward uniformity, while an attention attraction objective draws subsequent frames toward these collapsed tokens to amplify corruption. We further construct two human-centric I2V protection benchmarks and conduct

aaba9e6b332c2478eefd28de.title_original: ECGWmark: Deep Watermarking for Electrocardiogram Signals
aaba9e6b332c2478eefd28de.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13357v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Secure transmission of electrocardiogram (ECG) signals remains a major challenge in telecardiology. While traditional mathematical watermarking can embed patient metadata directly into ECG signals, it is highly fragile against temporal desynchronization such as circular phase shifts. In contrast, existing deep watermarking approaches for temporal signals, such as audio, typically rely on lossy quantization, which compromises the high-frequency micro-morphological details critical for clinical diagnosis. To bridge this gap, we propose ECGWmark, a fully convolutional and quantization-free deep watermarking framework for medical time-series. ECGWmark operates in a continuous, full-resolution latent space and utilizes a localized frame-level mechanism to improve the robustness to severe desynchronization. Crucially, we introduce a differentiable Physiological Loss guided by a clinical classifier to preserve diagnostic semantics. Experiments on the benchmark MIT-BIH database show that ECGWmark maintains channel-bit extraction accuracy above 90% under the evaluated circular temporal shifts. Furthermore, under a rigorous inter-patient diagnostic evaluation, Class-V sensitivity changes from 71.97% to 76.50%, whereas Macro-F1 changes from 35.25% to 34.71% and Class-S sensitivity from 8.89% to 1.39%; these results indicate mixed class-level effects.

62d66f4c37cdeab5ace5cf6c.title_original: AI Models Can Provably Hide Arbitrary Capabilities
62d66f4c37cdeab5ace5cf6c.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13928v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Capability evaluations aim to surface dangerous model behaviors before deployment, but their reliability depends on the assumption that hidden capabilities can be elicited. We show this assumption does not hold under adversarial conditions by constructing backdoor attacks that embed encrypted neural networks within host model weights, decrypting and executing them only upon receiving a secret trigger. Using digital lockers, these hidden circuits remain provably hard to elicit and interpret under cryptographic assumptions, even given full access to model weights, extending prior work from hiding fixed strings to arbitrary computations. We implement our proof of concept constructions in PyTorch and evaluate elicitation through fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search, and latent adversarial training on a small chemical reaction prediction task - a proxy for CBRN-relevant capabilities. Our results demonstrate resistance to these methods and, together with our cryptographic guarantees, reveal a limit of elicitation-based capability audits. We release our models to support the improvement of defenses.

a7ca693931cae11dbea97ea1.title_original: The Express Lane to Spam and Centralization: An Empirical Analysis of Arbitrum's Timeboost
a7ca693931cae11dbea97ea1.excerpt: arXiv:2509.22143v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: DeFi applications are vulnerable to MEV, where specialized actors profit by reordering or inserting transactions. To mitigate latency races and internalize MEV revenue, Arbitrum introduced Timeboost, an auction-based transaction sequencing mechanism that grants short-term priority access to an express lane. In this paper, we present the first large-scale empirical study of Timeboost, analyzing over 48.5 million express lane transactions and 494 thousand auctions between January 2025 and April 2026. Our results reveal five main findings. First, express lane control is highly centralized, with three entities winning 99.74% of auctions. Second, while express lane access provides earlier inclusion, it is currently mainly used for CEX-DEX arbitrage, limiting the value of priority access for other types of MEV extraction. Third, approximately 30% of timeboosted transactions revert, indicating that Timeboost does not effectively mitigate MEV inefficiencies such as spam. Fourth, secondary markets for reselling express lane rights struggle to sustain themselves due to poor execution reliability and unsustainable economics. Finally, auction competition declined as secondary markets introduced dedicated CEX-DEX execution lanes, enabling pay-per-transaction instead of pay-per-round billing and leading to steadily reduced revenue for the Arbitrum DAO. Taken together, these findings show that Timeboost fails to deliver on its stated goals

8ed7aece94edeaa089cdd047.title_original: A Comprehensive Survey of Website Fingerprinting Attacks and Defenses in Tor: Advances and Open Challenges
8ed7aece94edeaa089cdd047.excerpt: arXiv:2510.11804v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Tor network provides users with strong anonymity by routing their internet traffic through multiple relays. While Tor encrypts traffic and hides IP addresses, it remains vulnerable to traffic analysis attacks such as the website fingerprinting (WF) attack, achieving increasingly high fingerprinting accuracy even under open-world conditions. In response, researchers have proposed a variety of defenses, ranging from adaptive padding, traffic regularization, and traffic morphing to adversarial perturbation, that seek to obfuscate or reshape traffic traces. However, these defenses often entail trade-offs between privacy, usability, and system performance. Despite extensive research, a comprehensive survey unifying WF datasets, attack methodologies, and defense strategies remains absent. This paper fills that gap by systematically categorizing existing WF research into three key domains: datasets, attack models, and defense mechanisms. We provide an in-depth comparative analysis of techniques, highlight their strengths and limitations under diverse threat models, and discuss emerging challenges such as multi-tab browsing and coarse-grained traffic features. By consolidating prior work and identifying open research directions, this survey serves as a foundation for advancing stronger privacy protection in Tor.

0bc7ca4318a902a8734f63c0.title_original: Single-Shuffle Full-Open Card-Based Secure Computation Protocols for Any Function
0bc7ca4318a902a8734f63c0.excerpt: arXiv:2510.17308v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A card-based secure computation protocol is a method for $n$ parties to compute a function $f$ on their private inputs $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ using physical playing cards, in such a way that the suits of revealed cards leak no information beyond the value of $f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$. A \textit{single-shuffle full-open} protocol is a minimal model of card-based secure computation in which, after the parties place face-down cards representing their inputs, a single shuffle operation is performed and then all cards are opened to derive the output. Despite the simplicity of this model, the class of functions known to admit single-shuffle full-open protocols has been limited to a few small examples. In this work, we prove for the first time that every function admits a single-shuffle full-open protocol. We present two constructions that offer a trade-off between the number of cards and the complexity of the shuffle operation. These feasibility results are derived from a novel connection between single-shuffle full-open protocols and a cryptographic primitive known as \textit{Private Simultaneous Messages} protocols, which has rarely been studied in the context of card-based cryptography. We also present variants of single-shuffle protocols in which only a subset of cards are revealed. These protocols reduce the complexity of the shuffle operation compared to existing protocols in the same setting.

f0c538c6be1277fb3afc8bf8.title_original: RPP: A Certified Poisoned-Sample Detection Framework for Backdoor Attacks under Dataset Imbalance
f0c538c6be1277fb3afc8bf8.excerpt: arXiv:2602.00183v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deep neural networks are highly susceptible to backdoor attacks, yet most defense methods to date rely on balanced data, overlooking the pervasive class imbalance in real-world scenarios that can amplify backdoor threats. This paper presents the first in-depth investigation of how the dataset imbalance amplifies backdoor vulnerability, showing that (i) the imbalance induces a majority-class bias that increases susceptibility and (ii) conventional defenses degrade significantly as the imbalance grows. To address this, we propose Randomized Probability Perturbation (RPP), a certified poisoned-sample detection framework that operates in a black-box setting using only model output probabilities. For any inspected sample, RPP determines whether the input has been backdoor-manipulated, while offering provable within-domain detectability guarantees and a probabilistic upper bound on the false positive rate. Extensive experiments on five benchmarks (MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10, TinyImageNet and ImageNet10) covering 10 backdoor attacks and 12 baseline defenses show that RPP achieves significantly higher detection accuracy than state-of-the-art defenses, particularly under dataset imbalance. RPP establishes a theoretical and practical foundation for defending against backdoor attacks in real-world environments with imbalanced data.

b0fca8b3e05834b1a6bcd63f.title_original: TENNOR: Trustworthy Execution for Neural Networks through Obliviousness and Retrievals
b0fca8b3e05834b1a6bcd63f.excerpt: arXiv:2605.07160v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Training neural networks on sensitive data in untrusted cloud environments requires simultaneously achieving computational efficiency and rigorous privacy guarantees. Sparsification techniques, essential for scalable training of wide layers, expose input-dependent memory-access patterns that are visible and can be exploited by a host OS/hypervisor, even when computation is protected by a Trusted Execution Environment. We present TENNOR, a system that resolves this tension by co-designing the neural network training pipeline with doubly oblivious primitives, eliminating value-dependent neural network access-pattern leakage while also utilizing adaptive sparsification. TENNOR recasts sparse neuron activation as a locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) retrieval problem, reducing secure sparsification to doubly oblivious accesses over an LSH data structure. To eliminate the prohibitive storage cost of "multi-table" LSH, we introduce Multi-Probe Winner-Take-All (MP-WTA): the first multi-probe scheme for rank-based LSH, achieving a $50\times$ reduction in (hash table) memory while preserving model accuracy. We evaluate TENNOR on multi-label classification benchmarks, with output layers of up to hundreds of thousands of neurons under different batch sizes inside an Intel TDX Trusted Domain, achieving per-batch training speedups of $13\times$-$470\times$ over a Path ORAM baseline and reducing a 208-hour run to about 26 minutes.

e08aac056b1550114f53ec10.title_original: Beyond Edge Coverage: Per-Task Data-Flow Extraction at Kernel Function Boundaries via LLVM
e08aac056b1550114f53ec10.excerpt: arXiv:2606.00455v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Coverage-guided kernel fuzzers such as syzkaller rely on edge coverage trace-pc as their sole feedback signal. This context-blind approach cannot distinguish execution paths that differ only in argument values. For example, two invocations of copy_from_user() with different size parameters hit identical basic blocks yet have vastly different security implications. I present, an LLVM-based instrumentation framework that extends Linux KCOV with data-flow extraction of function arguments and return values. A compiler pass emits lightweight callbacks that report one source-level parameter per call, passing the value itself in a register together with its index and byte size. A composite is instead reported by the address of the object holding it, paired with a constant table of field (offset, size) pairs derived from DWARF DICompositeType metadata, with zero source annotation. The callbacks carry no program counter. The kernel derives it from the return address, which also attributes records the compiler emitted from inside an inlined body to the callee that was inlined. A lock-free per-task record buffer delivers variable-length records to user space with no interference to existing KCOV or syzkaller infrastructure, carrying entry, return, and comparison-operand records in one unified stream. 0c455eb3532f60f4ff48cbe7.title_original: Privacy-Preserving Intent Fulfilment and Assurance for 6G RAN
0c455eb3532f60f4ff48cbe7.excerpt: arXiv:2607.08809v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Intent-based network management automates 6G service lifecycles, but existing fulfilment and assurance approaches require traffic inspection, per-flow tracking, or vendor-internal telemetry. These requirements conflict with privacy constraints in multi-tenant networks and vendor opacity in O-RAN deployments. We present an architecture that provisions resources from declared intent categories without traffic inspection and verifies fulfilment using only cell-level standardised PM counters at the O1 interface. A data-processing inequality bounds resource-allocation leakage about traffic content by $\log_2 K$ bits for $K$ categories. Intent-traffic unlinkability and node-opaque verification hold by construction. If verification requires at least $q$ cells per category among $M$ cells, the ceiling becomes $\log_2 \lfloor M/q \rfloor$ bits. This bound covers the category/resource channel, not total inference from PM counters. When individual records add state-independent noise to the category aggregate, the category-mean verifier is at least as powerful as any per-agent verifier. We map the architecture to the 3GPP intent lifecycle and O-RAN Non-RT RIC. On production PM data from four operator networks, the category-mean score has higher AUC on three networks and comparable AUC on the fourth under category-wide replacement, while per-cell screening suits sparse faults. These injection-based experiments do not establish the theore

fa2d4d4f713c62dc3a9277d7.title_original: Two Birds One Stone: Effective Static Detection of Resource and Communication Deadlocks in Rust Programs
fa2d4d4f713c62dc3a9277d7.excerpt: arXiv:2401.01114v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Although Rust claims to enable fearless concurrency, concurrency errors remain prevalent in practical applications, with deadlocks particularly prominent and harmful. Current static deadlock detection techniques either do not cater to Rust programs without incorporating Rust semantics or solely concentrate on resource deadlocks, disregarding communication deadlocks. In this paper, we present RcChecker, the first static detection method that simultaneously targets resource and communication deadlocks for Rust. At its core, RcChecker introduces the signal-lock graph to characterize the interactions between threads through lock variables and condition variables. The construction of the signal-lock graph involves utilizing flow-sensitive and context-sensitive analyses to track variable lifetime details and abstracting actions associated with condition variables into signal resource holdings and requests. By examining cycles within the signal-lock graph, we can effectively identify resource and communication deadlocks in a unified way. Compared to the existing Rust deadlock detection tool, RcChecker effectively eliminates eight resource deadlock false positives and detects seventeen errors that the existing tool fails to identify. Furthermore, RcChecker reports seven previously undiscovered issues in real-world Rust applications, including two resource deadlocks and five communication deadlocks.

0763807fe23980f7eee29c82.title_original: An introduction to local differential privacy protocols using block designs
0763807fe23980f7eee29c82.excerpt: arXiv:2602.02744v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The design of protocols for local differential privacy (or LDP) has been a topic of considerable research interest in recent years. LDP protocols utilise the randomised encoding of outcomes of an experiment using a transition probability matrix (TPM). Several authors have observed that balanced incomplete block designs (BIBDs) provide nice examples of TPMs for LDP protocols. Indeed, it has been shown that such BIBD-based LDP protocols provide optimal estimators. In this primarily expository paper, we give a detailed introduction to LDP protocols and their connections with block designs. We prove that a subclass of LDP protocols known as pure LDP protocols are equivalent to $(r,\lambda)$-designs (which contain balanced incomplete block designs as a special case). An unbiased estimator for an LDP scheme is a left inverse of the transition probability matrix. We show that the optimal estimators for BIBD-based TPMs are precisely those obtained from the Moore-Penrose inverse of the corresponding TPM. We also review some existing work on optimal LDP protocols in the context of pure protocols.

f99970e44ccd1875a9b4d347.title_original: A Multi-Scenario UAV RF Dataset with Real-World Acquisition and Signal Processing Benchmarking
f99970e44ccd1875a9b4d347.excerpt: arXiv:2603.00106v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a real-world multi-scenario unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) radio frequency (RF) dataset, namely DRFF-R2, which is collected using a dedicated acquisition platform under diverse operational conditions. All signals are acquired within a unified framework to ensure consistency in hardware configuration and environmental settings. The dataset is systematically organized into seven well-defined subsets corresponding to different operational and signal composition scenarios to facilitate structured experimentation. Each file follows a clearly annotated naming convention to enable convenient data indexing and reproducible analysis. The dataset contains RF recordings from 26 UAV units spanning 8 distinct models, captured across varying flight states, altitudes, speeds, acquisition days, and receiver configurations. By covering diverse acquisition settings and signal compositions, the dataset provides a comprehensive resource for future UAV RF signal research, including RF fingerprinting (RFF) identification, model-level recognition, flight state analysis, time-varying RFF study, and interference-aware signal processing.

4f6507ba03c9b1f04f90f5e6.title_original: Identity-Based Signing Shifts, Not Solves, Usability: Evidence from Five Identity-Based Signing Ecosystems
4f6507ba03c9b1f04f90f5e6.excerpt: arXiv:2603.17133v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Identity-based software signing tools aim to make software artifact provenance verifiable while reducing the burden of long-lived key management. These tools are becoming critical infrastructure for secure software supply chains and are increasingly embedded in build, deployment, and release workflows. However, there is limited cross-tool, longitudinal evidence about which usability problems arise in practice and how reported concerns change over time. This gap matters because unusable signing and verification workflows can reduce adoption or lead to misconfiguration, undermining intended integrity guarantees. We conducted the first mining-software-repositories study of five identity-based signing ecosystems with public development repositories: Sigstore, OpenPubKey, HashiCorp Vault, Keyfactor, and Notary v2. We analyzed approximately 3,900 GitHub issue discussions from November 2021 to November 2025. We coded each issue for reported usability concerns and affected surfaces, comparing patterns across tools and over time. Across ecosystems, reported concerns are especially prominent around CLI tooling, policy/configuration, and verification workflows. Longitudinal Poisson trend analysis shows that reported issue counts decline substantially for several repositories, increase for OpenPubKey, and show no statistically detectable overall trend for the Keyfactor repositories, while trajectories vary across concern types. CVE-2026-108682.description: A weakness has been identified in zhayujie CowAgent up to 2.1.6. The affected element is the function read of the file /upload of the component Web Console. This manipulation causes denial of service. It is possible to initiate the attack remotely. The exploit has been made available to the public and could be used for attacks. The vendor was contacted early about this disclosure but did not respond in any way.
CVE-2026-108682.summary_ko: zhayujie CowAgent 웹 콘솔의 업로드 기능에 원격으로 서비스 거부를 유발할 수 있는 취약점이 있습니다.

CVE-2026-108683.description: A security vulnerability has been detected in zhayujie CowAgent up to 2.1.9. The impacted element is an unknown function of the component Media Download Handler. Such manipulation leads to uncontrolled memory allocation. It is possible to launch the attack remotely. The exploit has been disclosed publicly and may be used. Upgrading to version 2.2.0 is sufficient to resolve this issue. The name of the patch is b7967210268fc4c0afea1078223e74e7e96a8a54. You should upgrade the affected component.
CVE-2026-108683.summary_ko: zhayujie CowAgent 미디어 다운로드 핸들러에서 제어되지 않는 메모리 할당을 유발하는 보안 취약점이 발견되었습니다.

CVE-2026-108684.description: A vulnerability was detected in erzhongxmu Jeewms up to 3.7. This affects the function getTreeData of the file src/main/java/com/jeecg/demo/controller/JeecgFormDemoController.java of the component Autocomplete Data Handler. Performing a manipulation of the argument searchVal results in sql injection. The attack can be initiated remotely. The patch is named 6e29bd57972a499e9c8a81a2dbe94d0d5cf23af0. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue.
CVE-2026-108684.summary_ko: erzhongxmu Jeewms 자동완성 데이터 핸들러의 searchVal 인수를 조작하여 SQL 인젝션을 실행할 수 있는 취약점이 있습니다.

CVE-2026-108866.description: JeecgBoot through 3.9.5 contains a missing authorization vulnerability that allows authenticated users to read any account's permissions via the queryUserAuths handler. Low-privileged attackers can supply an arbitrary userId parameter to retrieve another user's complete permission set and identify administrator accounts.
CVE-2026-108866.summary_ko: JeecgBoot에서 인증된 사용자가 queryUserAuths 핸들러를 통해 다른 계정의 권한 정보를 읽을 수 있는 권한 누락 취약점이 있습니다.

CVE-2026-108867.description: JeecgBoot through 3.9.5 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in the SystemApiController getUserRoleSetById handler that allows any authenticated user to read other users' role assignments. Low-privileged attackers can supply an arbitrary userId parameter to retrieve assigned role codes and identify administrator accounts without the system:user:queryUserRole permission.

CVE-2026-108868.description: JeecgBoot through 3.9.5 contains a missing authorization vulnerability that allows any authenticated user to publish templated system announcements via POST /sys/api/sendBusTemplateAnnouncement. Low-privileged attackers can supply templateCode, toUser, and a forged fromUser to send notifications to arbitrary users through WebSocket, DingTalk, WeCom, Feishu and UniPush channels.

CVE-2026-108869.description: JeecgBoot through 3.9.5 contains a missing authorization vulnerability that allows low-privileged authenticated users to send system announcements by calling POST /sys/api/sendSysAnnouncement. Attackers can supply arbitrary title, content, fromUser and toUser values to deliver forged announcements to any users via WebSocket, WeCom, DingTalk and Feishu.

CVE-2026-108870.description: JeecgBoot through 3.9.5 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in the SysRoleController saveDatarule handler that allows low-privileged authenticated users to modify role data rules. Attackers can send permissionId, roleId and dataRuleIds to overwrite data_rule_ids, clearing row-level filters to widen readable records or altering filtering for other roles.

CVE-2026-108871.description: JeecgBoot through 3.9.5 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in the saveDatarule handler of SysDepartRoleController that lets low-privileged authenticated users modify department role data rules. Attackers can send crafted permissionId, roleId and dataRuleIds values to overwrite data_rule_ids, widening row-level data access or altering filtering for other department roles.

CVE-2026-108872.description: JeecgBoot through 3.9.5 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in the batchEditUsers handler of SysUserController that allows any authenticated user to edit user department assignments. Low-privileged attackers can send PUT requests to /sys/user/batchEditUsers with arbitrary user and department ids to move users, including administrators, between departments and overwrite positions.

CVE-2026-108873.description: JeecgBoot through 3.9.5 contains a missing authorization vulnerability that allows low-privileged authenticated users to modify any department by calling PUT /sys/user/doUpdateDepartInfo. Attackers can supply a department id to rename or re-parent it and replace or remove its department heads without ownership or tenant checks.

CVE-2026-108874.description: JeecgBoot through 3.9.5 contains a missing authorization vulnerability that allows any authenticated user to assign or remove department heads by calling PUT /sys/user/changeDepartChargePerson. Low-privileged attackers can supply arbitrary userId, department id, and status values to make any user a department head, widening department-scoped views, or demote existing heads.

CVE-2026-108875.description: JeecgBoot through 3.9.5 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in the SysUserController addSysUserGroup handler that allows any authenticated user to modify user group membership. Low-privileged attackers can send POST requests with arbitrary user ids and a groupId to add any users to administrator-maintained groups without permission checks.

CVE-2026-108876.description: JeecgBoot through 3.9.5 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in the putCancelQuit handler of SysUserController, allowing any authenticated user to cancel user resignations. Low-privileged attackers can supply user ids and a tenantId parameter or X-Tenant-Id header to restore ended, pending, or refused tenant memberships to normal.

CVE-2026-108877.description: JeecgBoot through 3.9.5 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in AiragPromptsController that allows any authenticated user to delete AI prompt templates by calling DELETE /airag/prompts/delete. Low-privileged attackers can obtain template ids from the unguarded GET /airag/prompts/list endpoint and logically delete any user's prompt template, making it unavailable to all users.

CVE-2026-108878.description: JeecgBoot through 3.9.5 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in the AiragAppController queryById handler that allows low-privileged authenticated users to read any AI application configuration. Attackers can enumerate application ids via the unguarded /airag/app/listDict endpoint and query each id to obtain system prompts, memory prompts, model ids, knowledge base ids, and plugin bindings of other users' applications.

CVE-2026-108879.description: JeecgBoot through 3.9.5 contains an insecure direct object reference vulnerability in AiragBaseApiController that allows authenticated users to read other users' AI chat variables via the username parameter. Attackers can send POST requests to /airag/api/getChatVariable with a target appId, username, and variable name to retrieve stored chat memory values from Redis.

CVE-2026-108880.description: JeecgBoot through 3.9.5 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in the PUT /sys/dict/editDictByLowAppId endpoint that allows any authenticated user to modify low-code application dictionaries. Attackers can supply a dictionary's low_app_id, obtained from GET /sys/dict/list, via the lowAppId parameter or X-Low-App-ID header to rename dictionaries and replace their items.

CVE-2026-108881.description: JeecgBoot through 3.9.5 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in the getTenantPackInfo handler that allows any authenticated user to read other tenants' product pack membership. Low-privileged attackers can supply a tenantId and fixed packCode values such as superAdmin, accountAdmin or appAdmin to disclose administrator usernames, real names, phones and departments.

CVE-2026-108882.description: JeecgBoot through 3.9.5 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in the SysPositionController removeUserPosition handler that allows any authenticated user to remove position members. Low-privileged attackers can send DELETE requests with arbitrary userIds and positionId values to delete sys_user_position rows, detaching users from positions without logging.

CVE-2026-108883.description: JeecgBoot through 3.9.5 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in the editThirdAppConfig handler that allows any authenticated user to modify third-party application configurations. Low-privileged attackers can replace client id, client secret, agent id and corp id of DingTalk, WeCom or Feishu integrations to redirect directory synchronisation and messaging to attacker-controlled applications or break them.
CVE-2026-108883.summary_ko: JeecgBoot에 인증된 사용자가 타사 앱 구성을 수정할 수 있는 권한 부재 취약점이 존재합니다.

CVE-2026-108885.description: JeecgBoot through 3.9.5 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in the SysMessageController delete handler that allows low-privileged authenticated users to delete message records. Attackers can send DELETE requests with arbitrary id values to remove any sys_sms row, erasing records of sent notifications without ownership checks.

Low-privileged attackers can supply arbitrary userId values to obtain names, emails, phone numbers, employee numbers, department assignments, and staff lists of departments those users head.

CVE-2026-107761.description: Several Postiz endpoints return the complete database row of the record they operate on instead of only the fields the client needs. Two of them include secrets the caller is not meant to receive. The public API's channel delete returns the deleted integration row, including the channel's platform access token and refresh token. A third-party OAuth app permitted to delete a channel therefore receives that channel's social platform credentials and can use them against the connected account directly, outside Postiz. `GET /user/organizations` returns each organization row, including its API key, to every member of the organization. The API key is intended for admins only, so a member with a lower role can obtain it and call the public API on behalf of the organization. Both endpoints require a valid session, API key or OAuth token and are scoped to the caller's own organization. There is no anonymous access and no cross-tenant exposure.
CVE-2026-107761.summary_ko: Postiz의 일부 엔드포인트가 필요한 필드 대신 전체 데이터베이스 레코드를 반환하여 토큰 및 API 키 등 비밀 정보가 노출되는 취약점이 있습니다.
